paragraphs.text: How do we achieve the D-B-T-L cycle
Early identification of respiratory pathogens can support timely infection-prevention decisions. We used measurement to guide engineering iterations toward more reliable detection.

1.Wet Lab (A–C). System configuration (A1–A3), primer–crRNA selection (B1–B3), and fluorescence readout (C1–C3) underwent separate iterations. Matched fluorescence tests selected RSV Candidate 2 and guided reaction and reporter conditions.

2.Dry Lab (D–F). Sequence-ranking methods (D1–D4), reaction dynamics (E1–E3), and candidate-data construction (F1–F3) evolved through multiple iterations. The handoffs B1 → D4 → B2 → B3 and A1 → E1 → E2 → E3 → A2 connect modeling to wet-lab tests; experimental measurements, not predictions alone, determined what advanced.

3.Hardware (G–I). Optical acquisition (G1–G2), thermal control (H1–H2), and app readout (I1–I4) were developed through their own stages. Fluorescence readouts informed device design (C2 → G1; C3 → G2); position-level verification and the I3 reconnection checks remain incomplete or planned.
Human Practices (J). Audience feedback prompted educational revisions (J1 → J2 → J1). The proposed app-usability link (J1 → I4) has not yet been experimentally tested.

Sensitivity, specificity, repeatability, and matrix-interference tests establish the system's laboratory performance. These results provide a basis for community screening, although field validation remains necessary.
Explore our Engineering page for detailed DBTL iterations and cross-module connections.
